agent.system_template:
You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

//! ELF parsing: header, program headers, section headers, string tables and
//! notes. While parsing, byte ranges of interesting structures are recorded so
//! that the report generator can highlight them in the file dump.

use crate::fail::{check_index, slice};
use std::collections::HashMap;

pub const PT_INTERP: u32 = 3;
pub const PT_NOTE: u32 = 4;
pub const SHT_STRTAB: u32 = 3;
pub const SHT_NOBITS: u32 = 8;

/// Highlighted byte ranges. For every file offset we keep the list of span
/// classes opened there (in insertion order) and the number of spans closed
/// after the byte at that offset.
pub struct Ranges {
    file_len: usize,
    starts: HashMap<usize, Vec<String>>,
    ends: HashMap<usize, usize>,
}

impl Ranges {
    fn new(file_len: usize) -> Ranges {
        Ranges {
            file_len,
            starts: HashMap::new(),
            ends: HashMap::new(),
        }
    }

    fn add(&mut self, start: u64, len: u64, class: String) {
        let start = start as usize;
        let last = start.wrapping_add(len as usize).wrapping_sub(1);
        check_index(self.file_len, start, "src/elf/parser.rs:116:18");
        check_index(self.file_len, last, "src/elf/parser.rs:117:18");
        self.starts.entry(start).or_default().push(class);
        *self.ends.entry(last).or_insert(0) += 1;
    }

    pub fn opens_at(&self, pos: usize) -> Option<&Vec<String>> {
        self.starts.get(&pos)
    }

    pub fn closes_at(&self, pos: usize) -> usize {
        self.ends.get(&pos).copied().unwrap_or(0)
    }
}

I've written a from-scratch Rust reimplementation of `elfcat` 0.1.10, and on every input I tried its output is byte-for-byte identical to the original's. That covers the HTML report, stdout, stderr (ignoring the thread ID in panic messages, which changes from run to run) and exit codes. A fresh clone builds cleanly with `./compile.sh`, and that build gives the same results. Everything is committed; `target/`, `./executable` and generated `*.html` files are in `.gitignore`.

**What was compared against the original:**
- **Real binaries:** about 1,020 ELF files from the system (including 46 larger ones up to 41 MB) plus the multi-architecture, 32/64-bit, big/little-endian and core-dump samples in Go's `debug/elf/testdata`. All match. A separate one-off check on the 186 MB `libLLVM` library gave identical 877 MB reports, and mine ran in 6.6 s against the original's 10 s.
- **Crafted and fuzzed files:** about 150 hand-built test files and more than 40,000 generated ones. The generated files either mutate real binaries or build synthetic ELF files with overlapping segments and sections, odd note layouts, malformed string tables and truncation. All match.
- **Command line:** wrong argument counts, `-h`/`--help`/`-v`/`--version`, unreadable or missing files, directories, non-UTF-8 arguments and unwritable output locations. All match.

**Notable behaviours, worked out by experiment and reproduced on purpose:**
- **Highlighting:** the original records highlighted byte ranges in a fixed insertion order. At each byte it opens all spans starting there and closes one span per range ending there. When ranges overlap badly, this produces the same broken-but-deterministic HTML as the original.
- **Note parsing quirks:** the description is read at an unaligned offset, while each highlighted note area is padded to 4 bytes. Every PT_NOTE segment's info table lists all notes in the file, not just its own.
- **String tables:** in the listing, the first string is cut to its first character. For section names, a name at offset 0 that never hits a NUL comes out empty instead of crashing.
- **Crashes:** where the original panics on malformed input, I print the same message, source location and exit code 101, since the original's source locations can't be produced naturally. One message, the one for non-UTF-8 arguments, cites a location inside the Rust 1.92 standard library and is hard-coded.

**Limitations:**
- If `RUST_BACKTRACE` is set, the original's panic output includes a backtrace that I don't reproduce.
- `compile.sh` uses the installed Rust toolchain (looking in the usual cargo locations). It only tries to install one via rustup, which needs internet, if none is found.

**Layout:**
- `src/main.rs`: argument handling, reading the file, writing the report.
- `src/elf.rs`: ELF parsing and highlight ranges.
- `src/report.rs`: HTML generation.
- `src/fail.rs`: reproduces the original's crash messages.
- `src/tpl/`: the fixed CSS/JS parts of the page, copied from the original's output.
